title: Maternal serum vitamin D level in early pregnancy and risk for preeclampsia: A case-control study in Southern Sweden
abstract: BACKGROUND: Preeclampsia is considered a major cause of maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality. The aim of the present case-control study in Sweden was to assess the hypothesized association between low serum vitamin D concentrations in early pregnancy and the risk of developing preeclampsia since vitamin D may play a role in early placental development. METHODS: The study included 296 women diagnosed with preeclampsia (cases) and 580 healthy pregnant women (controls). Serum samples were obtained from a biobank of samples collected in early pregnancy including almost all pregnancies in Southern Sweden. Concentrations of 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 (vitamin D) were analyzed using liquid chromatography-tandem-mass-spectrometry (LC/MS/MS). The cases were divided into two categories: i) infants were born before gestational week 34 (early onset) and/or born small-for-gestational age (SGA)(n = 51), ii) and others defined as late onset (n = 245). Vitamin D concentrations were analyzed both as a continuous and a categorized variable. RESULTS: When all preeclampsia cases were included in the analyses no consistent patterns were observed. However, the median serum concentrations of vitamin D were significantly lower among the cases who were early onset and/or were born SGA (median 39.2 nmol/L, range 1.2-93.6) as compared to the controls (49.0 nmol/L, 0.1-219; p = 0.01). In addition, high concentrations were statistically significantly associated with a decreased risk of preeclampsia (>66.9 vs ≤30.1 nmol/L; crude OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.16-0.96). When potential confounders were included in the models the associations were even more pronounced. CONCLUSIONS: Our results support the hypothesis that vitamin D deficiency is a risk factor for preeclampsia, but only in preeclampsia cases who were early-onset and/or were born SGA. Preeclampsia is not a homogenous condition and more studies are needed before vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy can be recommended.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2023 PLoS ONE case-control study has already attracted measurable scholarly attention, with 24 citations and a field- and year-normalized standing in the top 10% of outputs. Its influence is also visible in downstream reuse: the record shows 25 documented reuse events, alongside a small but notable scite signal that includes one supporting citation statement.

Full narrative

The article examines whether low maternal serum vitamin D in early pregnancy is associated with later preeclampsia, addressing a clinically important question in obstetrics and maternal-fetal health. Published open access in PLoS ONE by a Lund University team and supported by Swedish and European funding, it has reached an audience that extends beyond a single niche, with citations appearing across journals such as PLoS ONE, Frontiers in Medicine, Nutrients, Scientific Reports, and Pregnancy Hypertension.

The citation record suggests that the study is being used as part of a broader research conversation on vitamin D and pregnancy complications. The citing literature is dominated by article-length work, but it also includes reviews and preprints, indicating that the paper is serving both as an empirical reference point and as background for synthesis. The citing set spans multiple countries and institutions, with particularly visible uptake in education and healthcare sectors, which is consistent with a topic that intersects clinical research, training, and guideline-oriented discussion.

The reuse evidence adds another layer of reach. Rather than remaining a single isolated article, the work has been incorporated into related scholarly outputs and even noted in a biomedical article mention in Europe PMC. The downstream papers that cite it cluster around vitamin D research and pregnancy-related outcomes, especially preeclampsia and related hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, reinforcing that the article is being used in the same substantive problem space it set out to study.

At the same time, the public-discourse record is thin: no online mentions are captured in the available event data, and scite records only a modest citation profile. That pattern does not weaken the scholarly signal already present; it simply suggests that the article’s impact has so far been concentrated in academic reuse rather than broader public conversation. Overall, the evidence points to a steadily accumulating contribution that is already well above the norm for its field and publication year.
